questions.prompt: Use the \(p\)-series test to decide whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2}\) converges or diverges.
questions.answer: We compare the series with the \(p\)-series form \(\sum 1/n^p\). Here \(p=2\). A \(p\)-series converges when \(p>1\). Since \(2>1\), the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.

questions.prompt: Use the \(p\)-series test to decide whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\) converges or diverges.
questions.answer: Rewrite the term as \(1/\sqrt{n}=1/n^{1/2}\). This is a \(p\)-series with \(p=1/2\). A \(p\)-series converges only when \(p>1\). Since \(1/2\le 1\), the series diverges.

questions.prompt: Use the geometric series test to decide whether \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^n\) converges or diverges.
questions.answer: This is a geometric series with common ratio \(r=3/4\). A geometric series converges when \(|r|<1\). Since \(|3/4|<1\), the series converges. Its sum would be \(1/(1-3/4)=4\), but the convergence decision is that the series converges.

questions.prompt: Use the nth-term test to decide whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n}{n+1}\) converges or diverges.
questions.answer: The nth-term test says that if \(\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n\ne 0\), then \(\sum a_n\) diverges. Here \(a_n=\frac{n}{n+1}\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(n\) gives \(a_n=\frac{1}{1+1/n}\), so \(a_n\to 1\). Since the terms do not tend to \(0\), the series diverges.

questions.prompt: Use comparison to decide whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2+1}\) converges or diverges.
questions.answer: We compare with the convergent \(p\)-series \(\sum 1/n^2\). For \(n\ge 1\), \(n^2+1\ge n^2\), so \(0<\frac{1}{n^2+1}\le\frac{1}{n^2}\). Since \(\sum 1/n^2\) converges, the comparison test shows that \(\sum\frac{1}{n^2+1}\) also converges.

questions.prompt: Use comparison to decide whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+1}}\) converges or diverges.
questions.answer: We compare with the harmonic series. For \(n\ge 1\), \(\sqrt{n^2+1}\le n+1\), so \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+1}}\ge\frac{1}{n+1}\). The shifted harmonic series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n+1}\) diverges. Since our positive terms are at least as large as a divergent positive series, the comparison test shows that \(\sum\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+1}}\) diverges.

questions.prompt: Use the ratio test to decide whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n!}{5^n}\) converges or diverges.
questions.answer: Let \(a_n=n!/5^n\). The ratio test uses \(\left|a_{n+1}/a_n\right|\). We compute \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\frac{(n+1)!}{5^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{5^n}{n!}=\frac{n+1}{5}\). As \(n\to\infty\), this ratio tends to \(\infty\), which is greater than \(1\). By the ratio test, the series diverges.

questions.prompt: Use the ratio test to decide whether \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{3^n}{n!}\) converges or diverges.
questions.answer: Let \(a_n=3^n/n!\). The ratio test uses \(\left|a_{n+1}/a_n\right|\). We compute \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\frac{3^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\cdot\frac{n!}{3^n}=\frac{3}{n+1}\). As \(n\to\infty\), this ratio tends to \(0\), which is less than \(1\). Therefore the series converges by the ratio test.

questions.prompt: Decide whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\) converges absolutely, converges conditionally, or diverges.
questions.answer: First check alternating convergence. The positive terms \(1/n\) decrease to \(0\), so the alternating series test shows that \(\sum (-1)^{n+1}/n\) converges. Next check absolute convergence: \(\sum |(-1)^{n+1}/n|=\sum 1/n\), the harmonic series, which diverges. Therefore the original series converges conditionally, not absolutely.

questions.prompt: Use the integral test to decide whether \(\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n\ln n}\) converges or diverges.
questions.answer: We apply the integral test to \(f(x)=1/(x\ln x)\), which is positive and decreasing for \(x\ge 2\). Compute \(\int_2^b\frac{1}{x\ln x}\,dx\). With \(u=\ln x\), \(du=dx/x\), so the integral is \(\int_{\ln 2}^{\ln b}\frac{1}{u}\,du=\ln(\ln b)-\ln(\ln 2)\). As \(b\to\infty\), \(\ln(\ln b)\to\infty\). Therefore the improper integral diverges, and by the integral test the series diverges.
